clinician.trajectory_summary: A 43-year-old man presented with acute right hypochondrial pain for 4 days. Initial workup showed elevated WBC and CRP, very high CA 19-9 (2016 U/ml), and normal liver function tests. CT scan and Bili-MRI revealed suspicious irregular and porcelain-like thickening of the gallbladder wall. Due to a presumptive diagnosis of gallbladder carcinoma, the patient underwent radical cholecystectomy (Glenn operation) three days after admission. Intraoperatively, a hard gallbladder with a thickened wall and contiguous infiltration of the liver was found. Histological examination of the resected specimen showed ulcerated mucosa surrounded by epithelioid cells mixed with rare giant Langerhans cells, without caseous necrosis. Based on these findings, the diagnosis of Gallbladder Tuberculosis (GT) was retained. Postoperatively, the patient had an uneventful recovery and was discharged on POD 5. He was started on a 6-month course of antitubercular therapy (isoniazid, rifampicin, ethambutol, and pyrazinamide) and was doing well at 9-month follow-up.
